analysis.title: Wall Street's Vol Nightmare
key_insights: Nomura's McElligott estimates $47bn of leveraged ETF selling into yesterday's close, potentially the second-largest daily rebalance in its historical dataset. About 86% of the selling exposure is in tech leadership and AI-related products.

Nomura estimates roughly $61bn of implied vol-control selling following Thursday's volatility shock. These strategies react with a lag, so selling may extend into subsequent sessions rather than hit immediately.
VVIX rose 45 points after an apparent all-clear triggered a hedge unwind and the market then reversed sharply, forcing traders to buy protection again.

Discretionary traders are front-running systematic deleveraging, leveraged ETF rebalancing and dealer hedging. Dealers hold roughly $7bn of negative gamma per 1% SPX move, which creates the risk of a self-reinforcing selling spiral.
The Market Ear cautions that the timing of dealer hedging is uncertain. Dealers may have already sold in anticipation, adjusted hedges intraday or cut exposure before the close.
Per Nomura, hedge funds are focused on protecting their remaining 2026 performance rather than adding risk. Forced sellers are becoming more aggressive while discretionary buyers lose appetite.
Nomura data show a large skew shift in Mag7 options, with downside protection becoming more expensive relative to upside calls.

sector_views.rationale: About 86% of the estimated $47bn leveraged ETF selling exposure sits in tech leadership and AI-related products.

risk_factors: Self-reinforcing selling spiral from dealer short-gamma hedging, leveraged ETF rebalancing and vol-control deleveraging.
Vol-control selling is lagged and may extend over several sessions.
Reduced hedge fund risk appetite leaves few discretionary buyers to absorb forced selling.
Uncertain timing of dealer hedging makes the flows hard to front-run.
